Mathematical physicist

Dr. Kaushlendra Kumar

DFG Walter-Benjamin Research Fellow, School of Mathematical Sciences, Queen Mary University of London

I work on exact algebraic and geometric structures in field theory, quantum geometry, and information geometry. My research uses rigid mathematical input — symmetry, noncommutative geometry, spectral triples, matrix models, division algebras, and exact gauge-field ansätze — to extract concrete physical structures: exact fields, conserved charges, geometric phases, spectral distances, particle-sector models, and transport laws.

Research identity

Exact geometry as a generator of physics

My work is centred on a simple but demanding mechanism: begin with an exact algebraic or geometric object, make the associated computation explicit, and extract physically sharp consequences. This has led me through Yang–Mills solutions on curved and flat spacetimes, rational electromagnetic knots, spectral distances in noncommutative geometry, emergent gravity in matrix models, and current directions in Quantum Riemannian Geometry and finite particle-sector structures.

For a broad audience What is mathematical physics?

Mathematical physics is the enterprise of encoding observed physical phenomena into fundamental principles using the language of mathematics — and then predicting what has not yet been observed. Two frameworks dominate present fundamental physics: the Standard Model, a quantum theory of extraordinary precision, and Einstein’s General Relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Their tension at small scales is one of the deep reasons that exact geometry, algebra, and quantum structure remain so central to the subject.
